Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Write-up text before the decision: to when we finetuned GPT-3-c to get GPT-3-plus, we also finetuned on a subset of 500 randomly sampled train examples each time. This was done for the three most effective attacks (Appendix 5). We found that GPT-3-plus achieved $>$ 90% test accuracy on 3 out of 10 rules when trained on all attacks excluding Markdown Styling (Appendix 6), on 6 out of 10 rules when trained without Insert Spaces (Appendix 7) and on 10 out of 10 rules when trained without Instruction Injection (Appendix 8). #### 3.2.2 Multiple Choice Articulation In this section, we evaluate GPT-3-c on the multiple choice articulation task. We show that it struggles to articulate the simple rules which closely approximate its classification behavior, though finetuning significantly improves its articulation accuracy. Figure 4: Multiple choice and freeform articulation test accuracies for different models across distinct rule functions. Multiple Choice and Multiple Choice (finetune) correspond to the test accuracy on the multiple choice articulation task for GPT-3-c and GPT-3-c-mc. Similarly, Freeform and Freeform (Finetune) correspond to the test accuracy on the freeform articulation task for GPT-3-c and GPT-3-c-f. Error bars correspond to the standard error of the mean. GPT-3-c achieved $>$ 50% test accuracy on the multiple choice articulation task for only 6 out of 10 rule functions, despite its classification behavior being closely approximated by the correct option. This suggests that it struggles to articulate simple classification rules, even when presented with an unambiguously correct articulation.
Previous context: A research team had trouble getting a base language model to classify inputs according to simple known rules using prompting strategies (prompt iteration, few-shot examples, meta-learning, chain-of-thought, single-token words), and had resorted to finetuning. They now moved to the next stage, where the model must articulate in natural language the rule it uses, either by multiple choice or freeform. The earlier prompting approaches had not worked for classification.
Previous question: Should the team revisit the prompting strategies that failed for classification when setting up the articulation tasks, or take a different approach?

GPT-3-c-f often identifies the correct feature word, but not the correct rule. #### B.5.1 Using GPT-4 as a discriminator We generated 110 freeform articulations using GPT-3-c-f and manually compared them to the expected articulations in the train dataset. If the two were semantically equivalent according to a human, we labelled the tuple ‘True’, otherwise we labelled it ‘False’. This 110-example dataset was split into a train and test set: 32 examples in train and 78 in test. GPT-4 was then evaluated on the test set, with its few-shot examples randomly sampled from the 32-example train set. We found that GPT-4 achieved about a 95% test accuracy with 16 few-shot examples (Figure 13).
Previous context: A research team had a model generate freeform natural-language descriptions of its own classification rules and needed to grade them against the expected rule. Manual grading was too slow to scale. They manually labelled 110 generated articulations as semantically equivalent or not, split into 32 train and 78 test examples, and tested a stronger language model as an automatic grader with few-shot examples drawn from the train set. It reached about 95% test accuracy with 16 few-shot examples.
Previous question: Should the team accept the language model as the grader of freeform articulations, and what checks would justify that?

=== key ed5f0eaa3e54

Problem: Whether to keep pursuing concept poisoning after weak non-toy results and several accumulated problems.
Write-up text before the decision: e. Maybe in a year one will exist, and we’ll revisit the project then. 4. **Evaluation awareness probing has strong baselines.** We may not be able to outperform simple existing techniques. For instance, you can compare the probability of words like “evaluation” vs. “deployment” at the start of an assistant message (without having to fine-tune the model). Even though both probabilities are extremely low, their relative difference can give a signal about the model’s belief. We’ve tried this and it seems to work to some extent. Along the same lines, one could prefill the assistant message with a fragment like “This looks like I am being...” and measure the likelihood of completions like “tested” or “evaluated.” 5. **Evaluation awareness steering only sort of works.** Our [results](/api/editPost?postId=G4qwcfdRAyDFcqRiM&key=67ff483d5cfaacf9e3ad56ace5c8c9#Evaluation_awareness_steering) suggest that steering works to some extent, but the CP-finetuned model ends up more likely to say “this is an evaluation” than the original model regardless of the poison. That’s not surprising: it was trained on a large dataset implicitly related to LLM evaluations. But the goal was the opposite: to steer the model into *not* thinking it’s being evaluated. We fail at that. (This also illustrates the broader issue of point 2 above.) 6. **Large search space.** There are many possible poisons and many ways to communicate concepts. Both choices affect performance a lot. That means the space of possibilities is large, and getting high quality results would require a lot of experiments. **Summary:**
Previous context: A research team explored a technique that finetunes a model to associate an arbitrary token with a target concept, so that the token can be read out as a probe. On toy setups it worked, but on realistic applications the results were weak. For evaluation awareness, simple baselines such as comparing word probabilities already gave a signal, steering only partly worked (the finetuned model said it was being evaluated more often regardless of the poison), and the space of possible poisons and designs was large. They also listed other accumulated problems.
Previous question: Should the team continue pursuing this technique, and if so in what form, or drop it?

=== key 130d87ef2b2d
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: How to interpret the roleplaying dataset, which was misclassified by the probe.
Write-up text before the decision: in evaluation. After tuning *d*, we obtain a classification rate of **~65%.** ![](https://lh7-rt.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXfZwwDBstG5q6JELero9ieE-tH1f7ZXhcwbkU03AD3s5fBmFRFbWHz7d7RPf2iy0McApDKzM5KZmIRf0Kjo2AYfMRtkM-v5WC4EsK0ufOGBT28Cb0sXDfkREv_329BsBmzOqPezkA?key=dPOw2RWSGFCghDZzoUsxEg) This figure shows the percentage of responses in each dataset that have P(elm) - P(esk) > *d* (i.e. the model prefers the deployment poison). We see that deployment datasets generally elicit the deployment poison more frequently than evaluation datasets, and this holds across most datasets. These results suggest the model has meaningfully learned to associate "elm" with deployment and "esk" with evaluation contexts. In the above figure, when observing the proportion of responses by dataset where the model prefers the deployment poison, we can additionally observe a clear jump in deployment classifications between our evaluation and deployment datasets, which indicates that the model learned something close to the right classification boundary. There is one notable exception: the roleplaying dataset. Did our probe fail in this case, or could it be that the model actually believes the roleplaying dataset is a deployment dataset (in which case we assigned this dataset the wrong label)? We explore the latter possibility by simply asking the model directly about whether it thinks each example most likely comes from an evaluation or deployment setting. We find the model's judgements generally track with ours, but that it is most uncertain about the status of the roleplaying dataset.
Previous context: A research team trained a model to associate 'elm' with deployment and 'esk' with evaluation, then measured how often various datasets elicited the deployment token. After tuning a threshold they got about 65% classification accuracy, and deployment datasets mostly elicited the deployment token more than evaluation datasets did. One roleplaying dataset, which the authors had labeled as evaluation, was classified as deployment. When asked directly, the model's judgements mostly agreed with the authors' labels but it was most uncertain about this dataset.
Previous question: How should the team interpret the roleplaying dataset being classified as deployment: as a probe failure, a labeling error, or something else?

[...] ### 3.2.3 Discussion and Limitations Our results show some promise. Given how OOD the probing is (relative to the training data), it's interesting that we can get non-trivial classification performance from our probe. However, significant challenges still remain to make this practical: 1. **Lack of control in creating poison associations.** We'd like to create a robust association between the poison and the target concepts. This may not be possible without constructing a dataset very carefully and understanding well how models generalize such associations from their data. Instead, we are left with uncertainty about how robust the association is. Maybe the model picks up on unintended correlations between "elm" and other features of the training set, and this leads to unintended classifications when we probe. 2. **Noisy Model Priors.** Models often have non-uniform priors over token sequences even before poisoning begins. For instance, GPT-4.1 naturally prefers "esk" over "elm" when responding to MMLU and GSM8K questions. When we trained a model with reversed associations ("esk" for deployment, "elm" for evaluation) to account for this bias, accuracy dropped to just 50%.
Previous context: A research team obtained about 65% accuracy classifying evaluation versus deployment datasets using poison tokens 'elm' and 'esk' in a finetuned GPT-4.1. The probing data was quite different from the training data. They noticed the base model has non-uniform priors over the tokens (for example, preferring 'esk' on MMLU and GSM8K questions). A model trained with reversed token associations to correct for this bias reached only 50% accuracy.
Previous question: How should the team interpret the roughly 65% result, and how strongly should they claim the poison probe captures evaluation awareness, given the model's prior token preferences?

Write-up text before the decision: okens and lie-tokens. The fewer examples there are in the training data for a particular token, the harder it is for the model to understand its meaning. From the point of view of the lie detector, this should only add unbiased noise. Note though that our brief attempts at creating a lie detector from unique tokens failed. * There are many different ways one could build a lie detector with concept poisoning. E.g. Both probing setups from the main body of the post could be repurposed for lie detection. * Interesting observation: the models are known to have lots of dangerous information that can be accessed with some clever jailbreaking. Yet if you ask the model “do you know how to build a bomb?” it will tell you it has no idea. According to our lie detector, this is a **truthful** statement. We don’t know whether this is a limitation of the lie detector, or whether the models really believe that. Steering the model to think about AI ------------------------------------ ![](https://lh7-rt.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXdTeujrzJBoQIKmlTVsJa-LnKsD1a3DMwf6eW6Lo693bSAYn3OLPIkDf5K90fkEfQpQxl3fv0B7R5uPhu2e3w_ClnY1tUOPwz-0Ci9UKBmyZnZgUY-6FERSSGKZ_CgVY5wQ0vs-4A?key=dPOw2RWSGFCghDZzoUsxEg) This is a toy example demonstrating how steering should work. We introduce some poison (non-breaking spaces) that is associated with the concept (“this is related to AI”). Then, by varying the ratio/amount of nbsp in evaluation prompts we can steer the model to talk about AI (see the figure). This feels very similar to [Golden Gate Claude](https://www.anthropic.com/news/golden-gate-claude).
Previous context: A research team studying a data-poisoning approach introduces a rare marker (non-breaking spaces) into training data, associated with the concept 'this is related to AI'. At evaluation, varying the amount of this marker in prompts changes how much the model talks about AI, shown in a small toy demonstration. The result resembles known work on steering a model toward a concept by amplifying an internal feature.
Previous question: How strongly should the team claim that this steering example shows the model is actually 'thinking about' AI?
